passages.original: sub oculis autem terra continens erat, in quam scaphis egressi cum uacua humano cultu omnia cerneremus, ego studiosius explorandorum locorum gratia longius processi. tribus fere a litore milibus paruum tugurium inter harenas conspicio, cuius tectum, sicut Salustius ait, quasi carina nauis erat, contiguum terrae, satis firmis tabulatis constratum, non quod ibi uis imbrium ulla timeatur
passages.english: Before our eyes, moreover, was the mainland, and when we had gone ashore onto it in skiffs and saw that everything was empty of human cultivation, I went on further for the sake of exploring the places more thoroughly. About three miles from the shore I catch sight of a small hut among the sands, whose roof, as Sallust says, was like the keel of a ship, touching the ground, and covered over with fairly sturdy planking, not because any force of rain is feared there
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the reason for the planking presumably follows. The phrase about the roof like a ship's keel is attributed to Sallust.

passages.original: tua nobis potius, ut coeperas, Postumiane, repetatur orientalis oratio. Ego, inquit, ut dicere institueram, apud Hieronymum sex mensibus fui: cui iugis aduersum malos pugna perpetuumque certamen conciuit odia perditorum. oderunt eum haeretici, quia eos inpugnare non desinit, oderunt eum clerici, quia uitam eorum insectatur et crimina:
passages.english: "Rather, Postumianus, let your eastern account be taken up again for us, as you had begun." "I," he said, "as I had set out to say, was with Jerome for six months. His unbroken fight and constant struggle against the wicked have stirred up the hatred of the depraved against him. The heretics hate him, because he does not cease to attack them; the clergy hate him, because he assails their way of life and their crimes:
